definition: Stop words are the words in a stop list (or stoplist or negative dictionary) which are filtered out ("stopped") before or after processing of natural language data (i.e.
details: text) because they are deemed to have little semantic value or are otherwise insignificant for the task at hand. There is no single universal list of stop words used by all natural language processing (NLP) tools, nor any agreed upon rules for identifying stop words, and indeed not all tools even use such a list. Therefore, any group of words can be chosen as the stop words for a given purpose. The "general trend in [information retrieval] systems over time has been from standard use of quite large stop lists (200–300 terms) to very small stop lists (7–12 terms) to no stop list whatsoever".

explainer.lead: Stop words are common terms filtered out before or after text processing because they carry little task-specific meaning. Dropping them shrinks the data and speeds up retrieval and matching, at the cost of sometimes discarding signal.

tiers.eli5: Like skipping words such as "the" and "and" when you skim a page, because the meaning you need is in the other words.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers remove stop words to cut index size and speed up search or matching. Pitfall: there is no universal list, so a list tuned for one task can silently delete useful terms in another, such as phrases or negations.
tiers.paperLevel: A stop word is any word in a stop list (negative dictionary) removed before or after processing natural language text. No agreed rules or universal list exist, and not all tools use one; any word group can serve as the stop words for a given purpose.

explainer.example: A search index for support tickets strips "is", "the" and "my" so that only content words such as "login" and "error" are indexed.
